[Supreme Court]{.status .status-case} [548 U.S. 557](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-548/pdf/USREPORTS-548-557.pdf){.cite} [Decided June 29, 2006]{.cite} [5 to 3]{.cite}

**Holding.** No. The commissions' procedures violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice, which requires that commission rules match those of courts-martial as far as practicable, and Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. The Detainee Treatment Act's jurisdiction-stripping provision did not apply to pending cases.

**Question.** Whether the military commissions the President established by order to try Guantanamo detainees were lawful.

Background reading: [Wikipedia article on Hamdan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamdan_v._Rumsfeld) (secondary source).

## Why it matters

Hamdan made the scope of statutory authority, not inherent power, the decisive question, and so gave Congress the next move. It also confirmed that Common Article 3 applies to the conflict with al-Qaeda, which shaped detention and interrogation policy.

## How Congress responded

Within four months Congress enacted the [Military Commissions Act](../statutes/mil-commissions-2006.qmd), authorizing commissions by statute and barring habeas petitions from Guantanamo detainees, a provision later struck down in [Boumediene](../cases/boumediene-2008.qmd).

## Status

Good law as to its statutory holdings; the commissions now rest on the 2006 act as amended in 2009.

## Statutes at issue

- [UCMJ](../statutes/ucmj-1950.qmd){.subj}. Held the commissions failed the UCMJ's requirement that their procedures be uniform with courts-martial as far as practicable.
- [Detainee Treatment Act](../statutes/dta-2005.qmd){.subj}. Held its bar on habeas jurisdiction did not reach cases already pending.

Studied in [Unit 3: Deciding to use force](../study/units/war-powers.qmd).
